Medieval Feudalism. The dominant social, economic, and political system in Western Europe from the ninth to the fifteenth centuries. It emerged gradually during the early medieval period as local strongmen offered protection to peasants in exchange for their labor and loyalty, and this happened when centralized authority collapsed. Feudalism was built on a hierarchical network of mutual obligations between lords and vassals, where land ownership and military service formed the foundation of power and wealth.

Society organized itself into a pyramid: the king at the top, followed by great nobles, lesser knights, and at the bottom, peasants and serfs who were often bound to the land. The system was based on the exchange of land, called a fief, for military service and loyalty. A vassal swore homage to his lord and was bound by sacred oath to obey. This feudal contract was theoretically reciprocal—vassals owed service, but lords owed protection and fair governance, though in practice this balance shifted with power dynamics.

Feudalism fractured political power into thousands of small territories, each controlled by a feudal lord answerable only to his superior in the hierarchy. It also created a complex web of overlapping feudal relationships where a single lord could be vassal to multiple superiors, sometimes leading to conflicts of loyalty and civil wars. Land ownership became inextricably tied to military obligation and noble status, making landholding the primary source of both wealth and political authority.

The system began to decline after the Black Death dramatically reduced the peasant population, giving surviving serfs increased bargaining power and mobility. Over time, feudalism was gradually replaced by centralized national monarchies, professional armies, and commercial economies during the transition to the Renaissance. Though often romanticized as a chivalric order, feudalism was fundamentally a practical response to fragmentation of central authority following the fall of the Roman Empire. It shares historical connections with Medieval Europe, the broader period of which it was the defining characteristic, the Magna Carta which constrained feudal royal authority, Chivalry which gave feudalism its moral legitimacy, and England where it took root after the Norman Conquest.
